title: Issued USGS M1 postfire debris-flow likelihoods were about 3 times too high outside their southern California training records; ERA5-Land antecedent wetness did not explain it (western US)
abstract: Question: after western US wildfires, the USGS issues M1 debris-flow likelihoods for each stream segment. Does antecedent soil water change debris-flow odds when the M1 likelihood and the time since fire are fixed, and are the issued likelihoods reliable? Approach: we joined 3,616 field observations (Graber 2023/2024 USGS inventories, 23 fires, 510 storms) to the issued M1 terms of 23 assessments and computed M1 at the gage-measured peak 15-minute rainfall. We added the USGS v1 inventory (7,639 records, 77 fires, 2000-2025) and ERA5-Land soil water at the rain gage. The pre-registered test was a fire fixed-effect logistic model with storm permutations within fires. Results: 0-7 cm soil water gave an odds ratio per within-fire SD of 1.13 (95% CI 0.84-1.53, p = 0.47; 499 storms) and 0.84 (0.57-1.25, p = 0.49; 882 storms, 52 fires) in the v1 inventory. No wetness test of 17 reached p < 0.05. In year 1 after fire, the issued likelihoods predicted 945 debris flows where 305 were recorded (observed/expected 0.32, CI 0.25-0.39); segments rated 0.9-1.0 had debris flows in 46% of cases. Ratios fell to 0.09 in year 2 and 0.055 later. The M1 form refitted to its 817 southern California training records reproduces the published coefficients (observed/expected 1.00), but later records outside southern California gave 0.33 (0.26-0.40) in year 1. The observed log-odds rose about 0.3 times as steeply as M1 implies, also inside single storms and at rain gages within 0.5 km, so gage distance does not explain it. Discrimination was good (AUC 0.87). Limitations: inventories do not sample every segment; ERA5-Land is a 9 km model value; later southern California results depend mostly on two fires; the training split and slope checks are post hoc.
